clue.text: Rough sea still appears to have no bottom

indicators.note: rough water is churned up, so the letters of the next words are thrown into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A choppy sea seems bottomless to someone peering into it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rough' rearranges SEA and STILL. 'appears' is a link word: something that appears to have no bottom appears tailless.
explanation.definitionFit: A bottom is a tail end, so lacking a rear or tail means being without one.

clue.text: Instrument of torture used by Tom's gang?

definitions.meaning: a device for crushing the digits, used by torturers in past centuries
read as Tom ..., the band of the tiny folk-tale hero

explanation.surface: A torture device turns out to belong to a gang led by someone called Tom.
explanation.walkthrough: Tom Thumb is the tiny hero of an English folk tale; 'used by' is a link between the two readings.
explanation.definitionFit: The device squeezes the thumbs; the playful second reading splits the word into Thumb's crew.

clue.text: One Indian's abroad, living in Bali?

indicators.note: abroad means scattered widely, so the letters of the words before it are spread into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
read as the plain plural Indians, the apostrophe ignored, giving its final S

explanation.surface: An Indian person has gone overseas and is now living on the island of Bali.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in 'Indian's' is ignored so its S joins the fodder. 'abroad' rearranges ONE INDIANS.
explanation.definitionFit: Bali is an island of Indonesia, so a resident there is, by example, of that nationality.

clue.text: Glaringly coloured trumpet fish

parts.note: a lur is a long curved Bronze Age trumpet found in Scandinavia
the id or ide is a freshwater fish of the carp family

explanation.surface: A brightly coloured fish shaped like a trumpet.
explanation.definitionFit: Lurid describes colours that are harsh, vivid and garish.

clue.text: The operator used them to rotate stage

parts.note: to switch can mean to swing round or swap over, as in turning
the boards is a traditional name for the theatre stage

explanation.surface: A theatre technician used them to turn a revolving stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The boards' means the stage; the operator is a telephone operator, not a stage hand.
explanation.definitionFit: Telephone operators once connected calls by hand at these panels of plugs and sockets.

clue.text: She was hardly amused and made us petrified

indicators.note: petrified means frozen in shock, so the two words are jolted into a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An angry woman frightened us stiff.
explanation.walkthrough: The Gorgon of Greek myth turned onlookers to stone, so 'petrified' fits the surface too; 'hardly amused' also hints at an anagram of AMUSED, giving the same letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The snake-haired Gorgon of myth is pictured scowling and furious, hardly a figure of amusement.

clue.text: A Fowler, perhaps, spoiled Rene's date

indicators.note: a spoiled plan is messed up, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, the S included
taken as written

explanation.surface: A bird-catcher, perhaps, ruined Rene's romantic evening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fowler' looks like a bird-catcher but is Pauline Fowler, a long-running character in the BBC soap EastEnders, set in east London. 'spoiled' rearranges RENES DATE.
explanation.definitionFit: The Fowler family of the BBC soap are East Londoners, so one of them is an example.

clue.text: Part of your design is pointed

indicators.note: Part of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Some of your artwork comes to a point.
explanation.walkthrough: A rare heraldic term, best found from the hidden run and crossing letters.
explanation.definitionFit: In heraldry, a cross urde has arms ending in sharp points, so the term means pointed.

clue.text: A band of players into the bargain

parts.note: the LSO is the London Symphony Orchestra, a band of musicians

explanation.surface: A group of musicians thrown in as part of a deal.
explanation.definitionFit: Into the bargain is an idiom meaning in addition, as well.

clue.text: Support beneath centre of spine

parts.note: beneath means below, under

indicators.note: centre of picks the inner letters of spine, dropping its first and last

explanation.surface: Something supporting the middle of the backbone.
explanation.definitionFit: To underpin is to support from below, as with a foundation.

clue.text: Examples of indirect speech?

parts.note: not reported speech in grammar but stage remarks made to the audience, which the other characters supposedly cannot hear

explanation.surface: A grammar question about reported speech.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Indirect speech' suggests grammar; here it is lines in a play spoken to one side rather than directly to the other actors.
explanation.definitionFit: Remarks spoken apart from the main dialogue are indirect in the sense of not addressed straight to anyone onstage.

clue.text: Enduring quality of bare wheels in Detroit

definitions.meaning: the quality of never flagging or wearying
Americans spell tyre as tire, so wheels with no tyres have the condition of lacking tires

explanation.surface: Stamina displayed by cars stripped of their tyres in the Motor City.
explanation.walkthrough: Detroit points to American spelling: tyres are tires in the US.
explanation.definitionFit: Being untiring is endurance; the second reading jokes about wheels without tires.

clue.text: A cordial monk?

definitions.meaning: a cordial is a liqueur; this one is a herbal liqueur made in Normandy
a monk of the order founded by St Benedict

explanation.surface: A friendly monk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cordial' looks like the adjective friendly; it is the noun, a liqueur.
explanation.definitionFit: The French herbal liqueur shares its name with the monastic order said to have devised it.

clue.text: They show when and where index appears is newspaper

indicators.note: the index appears inside the newspaper's name, so one word is set within the other

parts.note: The Times is a British national newspaper
a table is a list or index, such as a table of contents

explanation.surface: Lists showing when and where an index can be found in a newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'appears is' signals the insertion, though 'is' reads like a slip for 'in'. 'where' belongs to the definition, not the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Transport schedules list the times and places of arrivals and departures.

clue.text: Holiday is on/off following withdrawals

indicators.note: following puts the rearranged letters after the holiday

parts.note: a recess is a break or holiday, as for Parliament

indicators.note: off means out of order, so the two letters pairs are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A holiday that keeps being switched on and off after people pull out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' rearranges the letters of 'is on'; the slash in 'on/off' is surface decoration, making the holiday sound intermittent.
explanation.definitionFit: A recession is the act of receding, so withdrawals is a synonym in the plural.

clue.text: Actors first seen in a musical

indicators.note: in puts that letter inside the musical's name

parts.note: Cats is the Andrew Lloyd Webber musical

indicators.note: first takes just the opening letter of seen

explanation.surface: Performers who first appeared in a stage musical.
explanation.walkthrough: The first letter of 'seen' goes inside CATS.
explanation.definitionFit: A cast is the company of actors in a production, so in the plural they are actors.

clue.text: Closures, say, shut down the presses

definitions.meaning: halts or shutdowns, for example of work
read as ..., an order to halt the printing

explanation.surface: Closures mean the printing presses are shut down.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading splits the word into STOP PAGES, as when a newspaper halts printing.
explanation.definitionFit: Stoppages are halts of work or blockages, of which closures are examples.

clue.text: Queue of those wanting a hole-in-the-wall?

definitions.text: Queue of those wanting a hole-in-the-wall?

parts.words: Queue of those wanting a hole-in-the-wall?
parts.note: a hole-in-the-wall is a British cash machine, and bread is slang for money, so a queue for cash

explanation.surface: People lining up at a cash machine.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'hole-in-the-wall' is British slang for a cash machine; bread is slang for money. The real sense is a line of poor people waiting for free food.
explanation.definitionFit: A line of needy people waiting for handouts of food, and figuratively the level of poverty.

clue.text: Is it eatable or for cooking? Tell me more

indicators.note: cooking is preparing food by mixing it up, so the letters of the words are mixed

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a dish is edible or meant to be cooked, and wants more detail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for cooking' rearranges EATABLE OR. 'Is it' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To elaborate is to add detail, which is what someone saying 'tell me more' asks for.

clue.text: Chaucer's steward with a tale about Eve

parts.note: re means concerning, about
taken as written

explanation.surface: A Chaucer pilgrim tells a story about the first woman.
explanation.walkthrough: The Reeve is one of the pilgrims in Chaucer's Canterbury Tales and tells The Reeve's Tale.
explanation.definitionFit: A reeve was a medieval estate steward, and Chaucer's pilgrim of that office tells a tale.

clue.text: They won't be taken for a ride

definitions.text: They won't be taken for a ride

parts.words: They won't be taken for a ride
parts.note: not people who refuse to be fooled but people travelling on foot, who ride in nothing

explanation.surface: People too shrewd to be fooled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taken for a ride' usually means cheated; here it is literal.
explanation.definitionFit: People going on foot are not carried anywhere, so they literally get no ride.

clue.text: Writer who lost half readership

indicators.note: losing half keeps only the first half of the letters of readership

explanation.surface: An author whose readership has dropped by half.
explanation.walkthrough: Charles Reade was a Victorian novelist, author of The Cloister and the Hearth.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Reade was a nineteenth-century English novelist and dramatist.

clue.text: Put together a variety of diet

indicators.note: a variety means a mix, so the four letters are mixed up

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Assembling a varied diet.
explanation.definitionFit: To edit is to assemble and arrange material, as in putting together a film.

clue.text: Leader of Eastern world, according to the Russians

parts.note: mir is the Russian word for world (and peace)

explanation.surface: The head of the Eastern world, as Russians see it.
explanation.definitionFit: An emir is a Muslim ruler or commander, so a leader.

clue.text: The cost of Mother's Day

parts.note: a dam is the mother of an animal, especially a horse
a day can mean a period or era, as in 'in my day', so an age

explanation.surface: How much Mother's Day ends up costing.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Damage is informal for cost, as in 'what's the damage?' when asking for the bill.

clue.text: Where ladies are at home in Mozart's opera

definitions.meaning: the women's quarters of a Muslim palace, a harem
The common English title of Mozart's Die Entfuhrung aus dem Serail

explanation.surface: A setting where women are at home in a Mozart opera.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means a harem, and is the usual name of Mozart's opera set in one.

clue.text: A songster's disease?

definitions.meaning: a songbird, as in the song ...
an infection caused by a yeast-like fungus

explanation.surface: A singer has caught an illness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'songster' looks like a singer but is a bird; the 's is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a speckled songbird and a fungal infection.

clue.text: Slanders occurring when prizes are announced

indicators.note: announced means spoken out, so the words are judged by their sound

parts.note: when means as, and purses are prize money, as in boxing

explanation.surface: Insults are traded when the winners are named.
explanation.walkthrough: AS (when) + PURSES (prizes) said aloud gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To asperse is to cast aspersions on, that is to slander or defame.
